title: E1: inherited run_tests skill on unseen bug-fix tasks
hypothesis: Executable inheritance helps small local models more than tools alone and more than the same knowledge as prose.

preregistered_verdicts.H1 skill tool vs tools-only: not attributable: the skill tool was called 1 time(s) and not by every agent
preregistered_verdicts.H2 skill tool vs prose recipe: not attributable: the skill tool was called 1 time(s) and not by every agent
preregistered_verdicts.H3 discovery waste with skill tool: not attributable: the skill tool was called 1 time(s) and not by every agent

limits: 4 tasks x 1 replicate per cell, temperature 0; effects under 2 tasks are inconclusive by preregistration. The controller arm was added after the first 12 Qwen runs (not preregistered) and is reported as exploratory.
finding: Offering the inherited skill as a tool did nothing measurable: Qwen never called it (0/4) and LFM called it once. The prose recipe was read (Qwen's test-discovery waste fell from 9 to 1) but did not change success beyond one task. What worked was having the runtime invoke the skill itself (E2 controller, added after preregistration, exploratory): 6/8 successes vs 3/8 tools-only; Qwen 4/4 with median 9 steps vs 13.5; LFM 2/4 vs 0/4 in every other arm, including the t1 pytest-without-pytest task both models otherwise failed. LFM2.5's dominant failure here was ending its turn with a JSON plan instead of tool calls; its 2.4x token speed did not become engineering success.
interpretation: Capability inheritance worked when the capability was wired into the controller, not when it was left to a small model's tool choice. That points the next experiments at controllers and routing, not at bigger tool menus.
